documents.title: Access Control Standard
documents.content:
Northstar Technologies
Access Control Standard
Document ID: NST-SEC-AC-001
Classification: Internal
Owner: Information Security
Version: 1.0

1. Purpose

This standard defines how Northstar Technologies grants, reviews, and removes access to company systems. It applies to employees, contractors, and any other identity that can log in to Northstar applications, infrastructure, or administrative tools.

Access control at Northstar is based on unique identities, least privilege, and timely removal of access that is no longer required. The requirements below are mandatory unless a written exception is approved by the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO).

2. Scope

This standard covers operating system accounts, directory accounts, application roles, cloud consoles, and privileged or break-glass identities. It does not replace the Authentication Standard, but it does overlap with it where privileged login protections are concerned.

3. Requirements

AC-01 Privileged multi-factor authentication
Privileged user accounts must use multi-factor authentication.
Privileged accounts include domain administrators, cloud tenant administrators, database administrators, security tool administrators, and any account that can change security settings or access production data without an application-level approval workflow. Password-only login is not acceptable for these accounts, including when connecting from the corporate network.

AC-02 Quarterly access reviews
User access must be reviewed at least quarterly.
Each system owner must confirm that every active account still has a valid business need and that assigned roles remain the minimum required. Reviews must cover standard users and privileged users. Completing a review only for administrators, or only once per year, does not meet this requirement.

AC-03 Termination access revocation
Access must be revoked within 24 hours of employment termination.
The 24-hour clock starts when Human Resources records the worker as terminated or when a contractor engagement officially ends, whichever is earlier. Revocation includes directory login, VPN, email, source control, cloud consoles, and production application roles. Disabling an account at the next monthly cleanup cycle is not sufficient.

AC-04 Privileged access approval
Privileged access must be granted only through a documented approval process that includes both the requestor’s manager and a security owner.
The security owner is the Information Security team or a named application security owner. Approvals must be recorded before the privilege is provisioned. Informal chat approval, after-the-fact justification, or manager-only approval does not satisfy this requirement.

AC-05 Unique interactive identities
Each person must use a unique user identifier for interactive login. Shared or generic accounts are prohibited for interactive use.
Service accounts used only by applications are permitted if they cannot be used for interactive login and are inventoried. Emergency break-glass accounts, if they exist, must still be attributed to a named individual when used and must not be a standing shared password used by a team.

4. Related controls

Privileged MFA in AC-01 is related to, but not the same as, remote-access MFA in the Authentication Standard. Quarterly reviews in AC-02 are related to termination handling in AC-03: a review finds stale access; termination should already have removed it. Logging of privileged activity may also appear in the Data Protection Standard; that logging does not replace the approval and uniqueness rules in this document.

5. Exceptions and review

Exceptions must be time-bounded, documented, and approved by the CISO. This standard is reviewed at least annually.

documents.title: Authentication Standard
documents.content:
Northstar Technologies
Authentication Standard
Document ID: NST-SEC-AUTH-001
Classification: Internal
Owner: Identity and Access Management
Version: 1.0

1. Purpose

This standard defines how users prove their identity when accessing Northstar Technologies systems. It covers remote access, password quality, account lockout, session lifetime, and password reuse. The goal is to reduce credential theft and limit the window in which a stolen password can be used.

2. Scope

This standard applies to workforce identities used for corporate applications, VPN, cloud consoles, and administrative interfaces. Customer-facing product login may follow a separate product standard; workforce access may not opt out of the requirements below.

3. Requirements

AUTH-01 Remote access multi-factor authentication
All remote access to corporate systems must require multi-factor authentication.
Remote access includes VPN, reverse proxies, cloud consoles reached from outside the office, and any split-tunnel or zero-trust access broker. MFA that applies only to VPN, while other remote paths remain password-only, does not meet this requirement. This control is related to privileged MFA in the Access Control Standard: privileged accounts always need MFA, and remote access needs MFA even for non-privileged users.

AUTH-02 Password length and compromised-password screening
Passwords must be at least 14 characters and must not be a password that has appeared in a known breach list.
Northstar must check new and changed passwords against a current compromised-password dataset (for example, a vendor-provided breach corpus or equivalent). Complexity rules such as “one uppercase letter” do not replace the 14-character minimum. Allowing shorter passwords for legacy systems, without a CISO exception, does not meet this requirement.

AUTH-03 Failed-attempt lockout
An account must be locked after five consecutive failed login attempts.
Lockout applies to directory, VPN, and applications that use Northstar single sign-on. Temporary lockout of at least 15 minutes, or until an administrator or automated identity workflow unlocks the account, is required. A warning message without lockout, or lockout only after ten failures, does not meet this requirement.

AUTH-04 Idle session timeout
Privileged sessions must time out after 15 minutes of inactivity. Standard user sessions must time out after 30 minutes of inactivity.
Timeout must end the session or require re-authentication. Screensaver locks on laptops do not satisfy this requirement for server consoles, cloud consoles, or web applications. This requirement is related to privileged access in the Access Control Standard: the stricter 15-minute timer applies whenever the session is privileged, even if the user originally authenticated with MFA.

AUTH-05 Password history
Reuse of the last 12 passwords is prohibited.
The identity system must reject a password change that matches any of the user’s previous 12 passwords. Advising users “not to reuse passwords” without technical enforcement does not meet this requirement.

4. Related controls

Authentication failures and lockouts should be visible to operations staff. Detailed query logs for production databases that hold customer personal data are specified in the Data Protection Standard; those logs are not a substitute for lockout and timeout. Incident response may treat repeated lockouts as a security event; reporting timelines are defined in the Incident Response Standard.

5. Exceptions and review

Protocol constraints that prevent 14-character passwords require a documented, time-bounded CISO exception and a compensating control. This standard is reviewed at least annually.

documents.title: Data Protection Standard
documents.content:
Northstar Technologies
Data Protection Standard
Document ID: NST-SEC-DP-001
Classification: Internal
Owner: Data Protection Office / Information Security
Version: 1.0

1. Purpose

This standard defines how Northstar Technologies protects Confidential and Restricted information at rest, in transit, in backups, and in production database access logs. Customer personal data used in Northstar products is treated as Restricted unless a data-protection assessment assigns a lower classification.

2. Classification used in this standard

Confidential: internal information that would harm Northstar if disclosed (for example, unreleased financials, detailed architecture).
Restricted: customer personal data, authentication secrets, and similarly sensitive regulated data.

3. Requirements

DP-01 Encryption at rest
Data classified as Confidential or Restricted must be encrypted at rest using AES-256 or an equivalent algorithm approved by Information Security.
Full-disk encryption, database transparent encryption, or object-storage server-side encryption meets this requirement when the algorithm is AES-256 or equivalent and keys are not stored in the same location as the ciphertext in plaintext form. Stating that encryption should be used “where practical,” or encrypting only laptops, does not meet this requirement for Confidential or Restricted data in servers, databases, and object storage.

DP-02 Encryption in transit
Confidential data transmitted over public networks must use TLS 1.2 or higher.
Public networks include the internet and any path that leaves a Northstar-controlled data center or cloud VPC. TLS 1.0 or 1.1 is not acceptable. This requirement is related to remote access in the Authentication Standard: an encrypted VPN does not remove the need for TLS 1.2 or higher on application traffic that still crosses a public network.

DP-03 Production database access logging
Production databases that contain customer personal data must log query and access activity, and those logs must be retained for at least 12 months.
Logs must identify the authenticated principal (or service account), timestamp, and object or query sufficient to support an investigation. Infrastructure or firewall logs alone do not meet this requirement. This logging is related to privileged access in the Access Control Standard and to incident investigation in the Incident Response Standard; neither of those documents sets the 12-month retention period.

DP-04 Encrypted geographically separated backups
Backup media containing Confidential data must be encrypted and stored offsite or in a geographically separate region.
“Geographically separate” means a different metropolitan region or cloud region from the primary copy. Unencrypted tapes or snapshots stored in the same building as production do not meet this requirement. Encryption of backups is related to DP-01 but is independently required even when production storage is already encrypted.

4. Related controls

Access to decryption keys is privileged access and must follow the Access Control Standard. Lost backup media or suspected ciphertext exfiltration must be handled under the Incident Response Standard. Authentication logs required by the Authentication Standard (failed logins, lockouts) are not a substitute for database query logs in DP-03.

5. Exceptions and review

Algorithm exceptions require Information Security approval and a documented compensating control. This standard is reviewed at least annually.

documents.title: Incident Response Standard
documents.content:
Northstar Technologies
Incident Response Standard
Document ID: NST-SEC-IR-001
Classification: Internal
Owner: Security Operations
Version: 1.0

1. Purpose

This standard defines how Northstar Technologies reports, classifies, discloses, and reviews security incidents. Fast reporting protects customers and limits dwell time. After-action reviews exist so the same failure is less likely to repeat.

2. Scope

This standard applies to confirmed and suspected events affecting confidentiality, integrity, or availability of Northstar systems or data. It includes malware, account takeover, lost devices containing Confidential data, production misconfiguration, and privacy incidents involving customer personal data.

3. Requirements

IR-01 One-hour reporting to the Security Operations Center
Security incidents must be reported to the Security Operations Center (SOC) within one hour of detection.
Detection means the point at which a workforce member, monitoring alert, or vendor first has a reasonable basis to believe a security incident may be occurring. Reporting “by the next business day,” or only after a manager reviews the event, does not meet this requirement. This timeline applies to all suspected security incidents, not only high-severity events.

IR-02 Severity classification within two hours
A documented incident severity classification (Sev 1 through Sev 4) must be applied to every incident within two hours of the report to the SOC.
Sev 1: active customer data exposure or widespread production outage caused by a security event.
Sev 2: significant security impact with a credible path to customer harm or material downtime.
Sev 3: limited impact, contained, no evidence of customer data exposure.
Sev 4: suspected event later confirmed as a false positive or negligible risk.
Leaving severity blank overnight, or using informal labels such as “pretty bad,” does not meet this requirement. Severity may later be upgraded or downgraded with a timestamped note.

IR-03 Seventy-two-hour customer notification
Customers must be notified of a confirmed confidentiality breach involving their personal data within 72 hours of confirmation.
Confirmation is the documented decision that unauthorized access to or disclosure of that customer’s personal data occurred. “Notify in a timely manner” without a 72-hour clock does not meet this requirement. Legal hold or law-enforcement delay requires CISO and counsel approval and must be recorded.

IR-04 After-action reviews for Sev 1 and Sev 2
After-action reviews must be completed within 10 business days of incident closure for Sev 1 and Sev 2 incidents.
The review must record root cause, timeline, what worked, and assigned follow-up owners. Optional lessons-learned meetings “as time allows,” or reviews only for Sev 1, do not meet this requirement. Sev 3 and Sev 4 reviews are encouraged but not required by this standard.

4. Related controls

Investigations will often need database access logs from the Data Protection Standard and authentication lockout data from the Authentication Standard. Privileged account misuse is also an access-control issue; reporting still follows IR-01 even when the Access Control Standard is the long-term fix.

5. Exceptions and review

This standard is reviewed at least annually or after any Sev 1 incident.

documents.title: Information Security Policy V1
documents.content:
Northstar Technologies
Information Security Policy
Version: 1.0
Effective: 4 March 2024
Owner: Chief Information Security Officer
Classification: Internal

1. Introduction

Northstar Technologies (“Northstar”) builds analytics software for mid-market customers. This Information Security Policy describes how we protect company and customer information. All employees and contractors who use Northstar systems are expected to follow it. Related procedures may be published by Information Security; where this policy is silent, teams should use reasonable professional judgment and escalate questions to the CISO.

2. Identities and access

Every person who logs in to Northstar systems must have a unique user identifier. Shared logins for day-to-day interactive use are not allowed. Application service accounts may exist where a system, not a person, needs to authenticate, provided those accounts are not used as a shared team password.

Privileged access — including domain administration, cloud tenant administration, and production database administration — must be requested in writing. The requestor’s manager and the Information Security team must both approve the request before the privilege is turned on. Privileged users must sign in with multi-factor authentication. Password-only privileged access is not permitted.

Remote access to the corporate network, including VPN and Northstar’s cloud administration portals from outside a Northstar office, also requires multi-factor authentication.

Managers should review the access of people on their teams at least once per year and remove access that is no longer needed. When someone leaves Northstar, Human Resources will notify IT, and IT will disable the person’s accounts within thirty (30) days of the last day of employment or contract.

3. Passwords and login protection

User passwords must be at least eight (8) characters and should include a mix of letters and numbers. Users are encouraged to choose memorable phrases rather than simple dictionary words.

After five consecutive failed login attempts, the account must be locked until Identity and Access Management unlocks it or until an automated cool-down of at least fifteen minutes has elapsed.

Laptop screen locks are required when staff step away from their desks. Application and console session lifetimes are left to product and infrastructure owners.

4. Protecting data

Northstar classifies information as Public, Internal, Confidential, or Restricted. Customer personal data is treated as Restricted.

Data sent over the internet or other public networks must be protected with TLS 1.2 or higher. Internal tools that still speak older TLS versions must be upgraded or isolated.

Encryption of data at rest should be used where practical, especially on company laptops. Server and database encryption is encouraged when it does not interfere with operations.

Backups of Confidential information must be encrypted. A copy of those backups must be stored in a cloud region or facility that is geographically separate from the primary production environment.

5. Detecting and handling incidents

Anyone who believes a security incident may be occurring must notify the Security Operations Center by the next business day. The SOC will assign a severity of Sev 1, Sev 2, Sev 3, or Sev 4 within two hours of receiving the report.

If Northstar confirms that a customer’s personal data was involved in a confidentiality breach, Customer Success and Legal will notify that customer as soon as practicable.

6. Policy administration

This policy is reviewed at least annually. Exceptions require CISO approval. Questions should be sent to security@northstar.example.

documents.title: Information Security Policy V2
documents.content:
Northstar Technologies
Information Security Policy
Version: 2.0
Effective: 12 January 2026
Owner: Chief Information Security Officer
Classification: Internal
Supersedes: Version 1.0 (4 March 2024)

1. Introduction

Northstar Technologies (“Northstar”) builds analytics software for mid-market customers. This Information Security Policy describes mandatory controls for workforce access, authentication, data protection, and incident handling. All employees and contractors who use Northstar systems must follow it. Product-specific customer login experiences are out of scope except where they store or process customer personal data on Northstar infrastructure.

2. Identities and access

Every person who logs in interactively must have a unique user identifier. Shared or generic accounts are prohibited for interactive use. Non-interactive service accounts are permitted if they cannot be used for human login and are recorded in the identity inventory.

Privileged access — including domain administration, cloud tenant administration, production database administration, and security-tool administration — must be requested in writing. The requestor’s manager and a security owner (Information Security or a named application security owner) must both approve the request before the privilege is provisioned. Privileged users must authenticate with multi-factor authentication; password-only privileged login is prohibited.

All remote access to corporate systems, including VPN, zero-trust access brokers, and cloud consoles used from outside a Northstar office, requires multi-factor authentication.

System owners must review user access at least quarterly, including both standard and privileged roles, and remove access that no longer has a business need.

When Human Resources records a termination, or when a contractor engagement ends, IT must revoke directory, VPN, email, source control, cloud console, and production application access within twenty-four (24) hours.

3. Passwords, lockout, and sessions

Passwords must be at least twelve (12) characters. Users should prefer passphrases. Identity and Access Management is encouraged to check new passwords against known-breach datasets when the identity platform makes that check available; the check is recommended, not mandatory, in this version of the policy.

Reuse of any of a user’s last twelve (12) passwords is prohibited, and the identity system must enforce that history check at password change.

After five consecutive failed login attempts, the account must be locked until Identity and Access Management unlocks it or until an automated cool-down of at least fifteen minutes has elapsed.

Privileged sessions must time out after fifteen (15) minutes of inactivity. Standard user sessions must time out after thirty (30) minutes of inactivity. Timeout must require re-authentication; a device screensaver alone is not sufficient for cloud consoles or web applications.

4. Protecting data

Northstar classifies information as Public, Internal, Confidential, or Restricted. Customer personal data is Restricted.

Confidential and Restricted data at rest — including servers, databases, and object storage, not only laptops — must be encrypted using AES-256 or another algorithm approved in writing by Information Security. Encryption keys must not be stored in plaintext beside the data they protect.

Confidential data transmitted over public networks must use TLS 1.2 or higher.

Backups that contain Confidential data must be encrypted and stored offsite or in a geographically separate region from the primary production copy.

5. Detecting and handling incidents

Sev 1 security incidents must be reported to the Security Operations Center within one hour of detection. All other suspected security incidents must be reported by the next business day.

The SOC must assign a documented severity of Sev 1, Sev 2, Sev 3, or Sev 4 within two hours of the report.

If Northstar confirms a confidentiality breach involving a customer’s personal data, that customer must be notified within seventy-two (72) hours of confirmation, unless counsel and the CISO record a legally required delay.

After-action reviews are required for Sev 1 incidents and must be completed within ten (10) business days of closure. After-action reviews for Sev 2 incidents are encouraged. Reviews should capture root cause and follow-up owners when they are performed.

6. Policy administration

This policy is reviewed at least annually and after any Sev 1 incident. Exceptions require time-bounded CISO approval. Questions should be sent to security@northstar.example.

requirements.title: One-hour reporting to the Security Operations Center
requirements.fullText:
IR-01 One-hour reporting to the Security Operations Center
Security incidents must be reported to the Security Operations Center (SOC) within one hour of detection.
Detection means the point at which a workforce member, monitoring alert, or vendor first has a reasonable basis to believe a security incident may be occurring. Reporting “by the next business day,” or only after a manager reviews the event, does not meet this requirement. This timeline applies to all suspected security incidents, not only high-severity events.

v1.reason: Incidents may be reported by the next business day, which is later than the one-hour SOC reporting requirement for all detections.
v1.evidence: Anyone who believes a security incident may be occurring must notify the Security Operations Center by the next business day.

v2.reason: Only Sev 1 incidents must be reported within one hour; all other suspected incidents may wait until the next business day, which contradicts the one-hour rule for every detection.
v2.evidence: Sev 1 security incidents must be reported to the Security Operations Center within one hour of detection. All other suspected security incidents must be reported by the next business day.

requirements.title: Severity classification within two hours
requirements.fullText:
IR-02 Severity classification within two hours
A documented incident severity classification (Sev 1 through Sev 4) must be applied to every incident within two hours of the report to the SOC.
Sev 1: active customer data exposure or widespread production outage caused by a security event.
Sev 2: significant security impact with a credible path to customer harm or material downtime.
Sev 3: limited impact, contained, no evidence of customer data exposure.
Sev 4: suspected event later confirmed as a false positive or negligible risk.
Leaving severity blank overnight, or using informal labels such as “pretty bad,” does not meet this requirement. Severity may later be upgraded or downgraded with a timestamped note.

v1.reason: Sev 1–4 must be assigned within two hours of the SOC receiving the report.
v1.evidence: The SOC will assign a severity of Sev 1, Sev 2, Sev 3, or Sev 4 within two hours of receiving the report.

v2.reason: Documented Sev 1–4 classification is still required within two hours of the report.
v2.evidence: The SOC must assign a documented severity of Sev 1, Sev 2, Sev 3, or Sev 4 within two hours of the report.

requirements.title: Seventy-two-hour customer notification
requirements.fullText:
IR-03 Seventy-two-hour customer notification
Customers must be notified of a confirmed confidentiality breach involving their personal data within 72 hours of confirmation.
Confirmation is the documented decision that unauthorized access to or disclosure of that customer’s personal data occurred. “Notify in a timely manner” without a 72-hour clock does not meet this requirement. Legal hold or law-enforcement delay requires CISO and counsel approval and must be recorded.

v1.reason: Customer notification is required after a confirmed personal-data confidentiality breach, but only 'as soon as practicable,' not within 72 hours of confirmation.
v1.evidence: If Northstar confirms that a customer’s personal data was involved in a confidentiality breach, Customer Success and Legal will notify that customer as soon as practicable.

v2.reason: Confirmed confidentiality breaches involving a customer’s personal data require notification within 72 hours of confirmation, with a recorded legal delay exception.
v2.evidence: If Northstar confirms a confidentiality breach involving a customer’s personal data, that customer must be notified within seventy-two (72) hours of confirmation, unless counsel and the CISO record a legally required delay.

requirements.title: After-action reviews for Sev 1 and Sev 2
requirements.fullText:
IR-04 After-action reviews for Sev 1 and Sev 2
After-action reviews must be completed within 10 business days of incident closure for Sev 1 and Sev 2 incidents.
The review must record root cause, timeline, what worked, and assigned follow-up owners. Optional lessons-learned meetings “as time allows,” or reviews only for Sev 1, do not meet this requirement. Sev 3 and Sev 4 reviews are encouraged but not required by this standard.

v1.reason: The policy does not require after-action reviews for Sev 1 or Sev 2 incidents or set a 10-business-day completion window.

v2.reason: After-action reviews are mandatory for Sev 1 within 10 business days, but only encouraged for Sev 2, so the Sev 2 half of the requirement is not met.
v2.evidence: After-action reviews are required for Sev 1 incidents and must be completed within ten (10) business days of closure. After-action reviews for Sev 2 incidents are encouraged.
